passages.title: Washing Pixel
sentences: On Sunday, Sam gave Pixel a bath.
First, he filled the tub with warm water.
Then Pixel jumped in the tub.
Sam washed Pixel with soap.
Next, Pixel jumped out and shook his fur.
Water went all over Sam.
Sam laughed and dried Pixel with a big towel.

passages.title: Maya's Rock Hunt
sentences: After school, Maya walked to the creek in Story Woods.
She looked for rocks by the water.
First, she found a gray rock.
Then she found a pink rock with small shiny spots.
She washed the pink rock in the creek.
At home, she put it in her rock box.
Maya smiled at her new rock.

passages.title: Leo Takes the Bus
sentences: Leo waited at the bus stop with his skateboard.
At ten in the morning, the bus came.
Leo got on and sat by the window.
The bus went past the library and the harbor.
Then it stopped at the skate park.
Leo got off and rode to the ramps.

passages.title: The Rover Race
sentences: On Friday, the robotics club held a rover race in the school gym.
Priya and Ben lined up their rovers at the start line.
Ms. Ortiz blew a whistle, and the race began.
Ben's rover went fast, but then it turned to the left.
It bumped into the wall and stopped.
Priya's rover kept going in a straight line.
It crossed the finish line first.
Priya cheered, and Ben helped her carry the rover back to the table.
Later, they fixed the wheel on Ben's rover together.

passages.title: The Dog and His Reflection
sentences: A dog found a big bone near a shop.
He held it in his mouth and walked home.
On the way, he crossed a small bridge over a river.
He looked down and saw a dog in the water.
That dog had a bone too, and it looked bigger.
The first dog wanted the bigger bone.
He opened his mouth to bark at the other dog.
His own bone fell into the river and sank.
The dog in the water was only his reflection.
He walked home with an empty mouth.

credit.title: The Dog and His Reflection
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Ferry to Shell Island
sentences: The ferry left the harbor at nine o'clock on Saturday morning.
Sam and Maya stood at the front and watched the waves.
Before they got on the ferry, Grandma Rose had given them two warm muffins from the bakery.
They ate the muffins as the ferry crossed the bay.
Twenty minutes later, the ferry stopped at Shell Island.
Maya ran to the rocky beach to look for green sea glass.
Sam opened his map and found a path to the old lighthouse.
Later, they walked the path together, and Maya filled her bag with shiny stones.
At noon, they rode the ferry back to Harbor Town.
On the way home, Maya showed Sam a smooth piece of green glass.

passages.title: Fixing the Chain
sentences: After school on Wednesday, Ben pushed his bike to Okafor's Bike Shop.
The chain had come off on the hill that morning.
Mr. Okafor lifted the bike onto a metal repair stand.
He showed Ben how to put the chain back on the gears.
Then Ben turned the pedals slowly, and the chain stayed on.
Mr. Okafor added a few drops of oil to the chain.
Ben thanked him and rode home along the harbor.
That night, Ben wrote the steps in his notebook so he could fix the chain by himself next time.

passages.title: Ana's Corner Kick
sentences: Ana scored the winning goal on Saturday afternoon.
She kicked the ball from the corner, and it curved into the net.
Earlier that week, she had practiced corner kicks with Ben every evening in the park.
On Monday, most of her kicks went too far.
By Thursday, she could curve the ball into the goal almost every time.
After the game on Saturday, the whole team walked to Rose's Bakery.
Grandma Rose gave Ana a cookie shaped like a soccer ball.
Ana ate half of it and gave the other half to Ben.

passages.title: Sam's Railway Model
sentences: On the morning of the library's model train show, an old man stopped at Sam's table and studied his model for a long time.
He told Sam that he had driven trains on the island many years ago.
Then he said that every curve on the model looked exactly right.
Sam felt proud, because those curves had taken longer than any other part.
Sam had started the model four weeks before the show.
First, he went to the library to study old maps of the railway that once carried stone from the quarry to the harbor.
A quarry is a deep pit where workers cut rock out of the ground.
Sam traced the route onto a large board, and then he painted the hills green and the sea blue.
Next, he glued down the tracks, one short piece at a time.
That step took two whole weeks, because each curve had to match the map.
When the glue was dry, Sam tested a small engine on the tracks, and it rolled all the way to the harbor without stopping.
The night before the show, he added one last detail.
Grandma Rose had painted a tiny sign for Rose's Bakery, and Sam glued it beside the station.

passages.title: Leo's Skate Video
sentences: Leo wanted to enter the Harbor Town skate video contest.
The rules said that each video had to be shorter than one minute and that it had to be sent in by six o'clock on Sunday.
On Saturday morning, Leo asked Sam to film him at the skate park, because Sam can hold a phone very still.
Sam stood by the low ramp with Leo's phone while Leo practiced a kickflip.
A seagull landed on the railing and watched them, and Leo joked that it was the contest judge.
Leo missed the landing on his first six tries.
On the seventh try, he landed the trick perfectly, and Sam filmed the whole thing.
That afternoon, the two boys sat in the Lighthouse Café and cut the video down to fifty seconds.
Sam chose music with a fast drum beat, and Leo drank a large hot chocolate.
On Sunday at noon, six hours before the end of the contest, Leo sent in his video.

passages.title: The Late Ferry
sentences: By the time the ferry finally left the harbor at two o'clock, Ana and Ben had already eaten lunch, played three games of cards and repaired a broken backpack strap.
None of that had been part of their plan.
Their day had started at seven o'clock that morning.
The twins were going to Gull Island to spend the weekend with their cousins, and their mother drove them to the harbor for the nine o'clock ferry.
When they reached the ticket window, they read a sign that said all morning ferries were cancelled because of strong wind out at sea.
The next ferry would leave at two o'clock, if the wind became calmer.
At first, Ben felt frustrated, because he had planned every hour of the weekend.
Then Ana suggested that they use the extra time instead of just waiting, and their mother agreed.
The three of them walked to the Lighthouse Café, where the twins ate grilled cheese sandwiches and watched the fishing boats rock in the harbor.
After lunch, the strap on Ana's backpack snapped, so Ben borrowed tape from the café owner and wrapped it tightly around the broken strap.
Then the twins played cards at a table by the window until they heard the ferry horn.
The wind was much calmer now, and the crossing took the usual forty minutes.
Their cousins were waiting on the dock at Gull Island, holding a big sign that said WELCOME.
Ben laughed and told them that a forty-minute trip had taken the whole day, but he agreed that it had still been a good day.

passages.title: A Night of Stars
sentences: On Friday night, Priya and her mom drove to the campsite in Story Woods.
First, they set up their tent beside the creek.
Then they ate hot soup by the fire.
When the sky was dark, Priya lay on a blanket and looked up.
She found the seven bright stars of the Big Dipper.
Next, her mom pointed to a small red dot low in the sky.
"That is the planet Mars," she said.
Before they went to sleep, Priya drew the stars in her notebook.

passages.title: Pizza Night
sentences: At six o'clock on Saturday, Sam and Grandma Rose took a hot pizza out of the oven.
The cheese was bubbling, and the crust was golden brown.
Making it had taken all afternoon.
At two o'clock, Grandma Rose mixed flour, water, salt and yeast into a soft dough.
Before that, Sam had walked to the market to buy peppers and a block of cheese.
Yeast is a tiny living thing that makes gas, and the gas makes dough puff up.
The dough sat in a warm bowl for three hours, and it grew to twice its size.
While it grew, Sam chopped the peppers and grated the cheese.
Next, he stretched the dough into a circle on a metal tray.
He spread tomato sauce on it and added the cheese and peppers.
Then Grandma Rose slid the tray into the hot oven.
Pixel sat by the oven door and watched the whole time.

passages.title: The Game Tournament
sentences: On Saturday afternoon, the library held a racing game tournament in its big meeting room.
Sixteen players sat in pairs in front of eight large screens.
The winner of each race moved on to the next round.
Ben won his first race by less than one second.
Then he lost his second race to an older student from Gull Island.
Ana won her first two races and reached the final.
Before the final started, she drank some water and stretched her fingers.
The last race was on a mountain track covered in snow.
Ana knew that track well.
She had practiced it every evening since Monday, when the twins signed up for the tournament.
She stayed on the inside of every corner and won by three seconds.
The librarian gave her a small gold cup, and Ben cheered louder than anyone in the room.

passages.title: The Fossil Dig
sentences: By four o'clock on Sunday, the fossil was safe in the back of the museum's truck, inside a hard white shell of plaster.
Maya and Grandma Rose had spent the whole day helping to dig it out of the clay cliffs north of Harbor Town.
It was a leg bone from a duck-billed dinosaur, a large plant eater that lived long before there were any people.
Their day had started at eight o'clock that morning, when they met Dr. Bell at the bottom of the cliffs.
Dr. Bell is a paleontologist, and her team had found the edge of the bone one week earlier.
First, she showed Maya how to scrape away the soft rock with a small metal tool, one thin layer at a time.
After two hours of careful work, the whole top of the bone could be seen.
Maya measured the bone with a tape and marked its exact place on a map of the cliff.
Before that, Grandma Rose had taken photos of the bone from every side.
At noon, they all ate cheese sandwiches on a flat rock and watched the waves.
After lunch came the hardest step.
Dr. Bell dipped strips of cloth in wet plaster, and Maya helped to lay them over the bone.
When the plaster dried, it made a hard jacket that would keep the fossil from breaking on the bumpy road.
Finally, four people lifted the jacket together and carried it carefully to the truck.

passages.title: The Piano at the Bakery
sentences: For thirty years, an old piano had stood in the back room of Rose's Bakery, hidden behind sacks of flour.
One day in April, Grandma Rose decided that it should be played again.
First, Mr. Okafor and Leo moved the sacks and rolled the piano into the front of the shop.
Before that, Mr. Okafor had oiled its four small wheels, because they had not turned in years.
Next, a piano tuner came to fix the sound.
Inside a piano, each key moves a small hammer that hits one or more tight strings.
The tuner turned metal pins to make each string a little tighter or looser, until every note sounded right.
The job took her three hours, and she drank two cups of coffee while she worked.
Then Ben began to learn a short song called "The Harbor Waltz."
He had only played a keyboard at school before, so he practiced for one hour every day for two weeks.
Grandma Rose let him practice in the early morning, before the bakery opened.
On the first Saturday in May, Ben played the song for the customers.
A man at the window table tapped his foot, and Pixel lay under the piano the whole time.
When the song ended, everyone clapped, and Grandma Rose asked Ben to play it again.

passages.title: The Robot Competition
sentences: With ninety seconds left on the clock, Priya's rover stopped in the middle of the course, and the crowd in the gym became very quiet.
Priya stayed calm, because she had seen this exact problem before.
The island robot competition had started at nine o'clock that morning in the gym at Harbor Middle School.
Each rover had to follow a black line across the floor, pick up three foam blocks and drop them into a box, all in less than four minutes.
The rovers follow the line with light sensors, because a black line reflects much less light than the white floor around it.
Priya's team had started building their rover in Ms. Ortiz's science room six weeks earlier.
Two weeks before the competition, during a test in that room, the rover had stopped in the same way.
After an hour of searching, Priya discovered that a thin layer of dust had covered its light sensor, so the sensor could no longer find the line.
Now, in the gym, she remembered that test.
The rules allowed each team one short repair during a run, so she raised her hand, and the judge nodded.
She lifted the rover, wiped the sensor with a soft cloth, and set it back on the line.
The rover rolled forward, picked up the last foam block and dropped it into the box with eleven seconds left on the clock.
Another team's rover finished faster, so Priya's team finished in second place.
However, the judges also gave them a prize for the best repair of the day.
That evening, Priya taped a small cloth inside the rover's lid, so it would always be ready for the next competition.

passages.title: The Treasure Hunt
sentences: On the first Saturday in October, the library held a treasure hunt in Story Woods.
Each team of three received a map of the woods, a compass and a card with the first clue.
A compass needle always points north, so a team that knows where north is can find every other direction.
Sam, Maya and Leo formed a team, and Sam carried the map, because he had spent an hour studying it the night before.
The first clue said to walk north from the campsite until they reached water.
They followed the compass needle and came to the creek after ten minutes.
A second card was tied to a tree beside the creek, and it told them to follow the water downhill to the old mill.
On the way, Leo stopped to look at a green frog, and Maya picked up a smooth black stone for her rock box.
At the mill, they found the third clue, which was a letter and a number: C4.
Sam unfolded the map and showed the others that C4 was one of the squares on its grid.
While Sam studied the grid, Maya made a quick drawing of the waterwheel for her next comic.
Then the team climbed a steep path into square C4, where they found a large flat rock.
Under the rock was a wooden box tied with a gold ribbon.
Inside were three gold library cards, which let each of them borrow ten books at a time instead of five.
Before they untied the ribbon, Leo had taken a photo of the closed box, so they would remember exactly where they found it.
They walked back to the campsite and learned that they were the second team to finish, just behind Ana and Ben.

passages.title: Maya's Flute
sentences: Maya took her flute out of its case.
First, she put the three parts together.
Then she held the flute up to her lips.
She blew across the small hole.
A soft, clear note came out.
Next, she played a short song.
At the end, she wiped the flute with a cloth.

passages.title: The Snow Fort
sentences: Snow fell all night.
In the morning, Ana and Ben ran out to the yard.
First, they rolled big balls of snow.
Then they piled the balls up to make a wall.
Ben cut a small door in the wall.
Next, Ana put a red flag on top.
The fort was done by lunch.

passages.title: The Bird Feeder
sentences: Sam got a new bird feeder.
First, he filled it with seeds.
Then he hung it on a tree in the yard.
Pixel sat by the back door and watched.
Soon, a red bird came to the feeder.
It ate some seeds.
Then it flew away.
Sam drew the bird in his notebook.

passages.title: The Comet Photo
sentences: On Tuesday night, Priya rode up to the observatory with her dad.
Dr. Hale met them at the door.
A comet was in the sky that week.
A comet is a ball of ice and dust that goes around the Sun.
First, Dr. Hale turned a telescope toward the comet.
Priya looked through it and saw a white spot with a long tail.
Then Dr. Hale took a photo with a camera on the telescope.
Next, she printed the photo for Priya.
At home, Priya hung it above her desk.

passages.title: The Tide Pool
sentences: On Sunday morning, the tide was low.
Sam and Maya walked to the rocks by the harbor.
First, they found a pool of water between two rocks.
A small crab ran under a stone.
Then Maya saw an orange sea star on the side of the pool.
Sam took a photo of it.
They left the sea star in the water, where it was safe.
Next, the water began to rise.
The tide was coming back in, so they walked home.

passages.title: Ben's Game Level
sentences: Ben played a new video game after dinner.
His hero had to get out of a castle.
First, the hero found a gold key under a table.
Then he jumped across three moving boxes.
Next, he pulled a lever, and a bridge came down.
The hero ran across the bridge.
At the end, he used the gold key to open the big door.
Ben saved the game and went to bed.

passages.title: Priya's Robot Arm
sentences: Priya built a small robot arm for the science fair.
She wanted it to pick up a cup and move it.
On Monday, she wrote the code on her laptop.
On Tuesday, she tested the arm, but it dropped the cup.
The grip was too loose.
On Wednesday, she put rubber pads on the grip.
Then she tested it again.
This time, the arm held the cup and set it down on a shelf.
Ms. Ortiz clapped when she saw it work.

passages.title: The Dinosaur Model
sentences: Maya got a model kit of a Triceratops skeleton.
Triceratops was a plant eater with three horns on its head.
First, Maya snapped the leg bones onto a stand.
Then she joined the long backbone to the legs.
Next, she added the ribs, one at a time.
Then she painted the horns on the skull light brown.
When the paint was dry, she pressed the skull onto the backbone.
She set the model on her shelf, next to her rock box.

passages.title: A Map for Leo
sentences: Sam's family was going away for three days, so Leo agreed to walk Pixel.
On Thursday, Sam made a map of their usual walk, so Leo would know the way.
Before he started to draw, he walked the route with Pixel one more time and wrote notes.
At home, he drew his house in the bottom corner of a big sheet of paper.
Next, he drew the path to the creek and a small bridge over the water.
After the bridge, the path turns left at a tall pine tree, so he drew the tree too.
Then he drew the fountain in the park, where Pixel always stops to drink.
Last, he added a red arrow that showed the way back home.
On Friday morning, he gave the map to Leo.
Leo studied it and said it was easier to read than his math book.

passages.title: Panning for Gold
sentences: At the mine museum, Mr. Varga showed the rock club how people once looked for gold in streams.
Each student got a shallow metal pan full of sand and gravel.
First, Maya lowered her pan into a long tub of water.
Then she shook the pan from side to side.
Gold is much heavier than sand, so the gold sank to the bottom of the pan.
Next, she tipped the pan a little and swirled the water around.
The light sand washed over the edge, one small wave at a time.
After ten minutes, only a spoonful of dark sand was left.
Maya looked closely and saw three tiny yellow flakes shining in it.
Mr. Varga helped her put the flakes into a small glass tube with water.
At home, she put the tube in her rock box, next to her best crystals.

passages.title: The Relay Race
sentences: On Sports Day, Ana, Priya, Leo and Sam ran the relay race for their team.
Each runner had to run once around the track and then pass a baton to the next runner.
A baton is a short stick that runners carry in one hand.
Ana ran first, and she was in second place when she reached Priya.
While Priya ran, Leo tied his shoe and Sam waved to Grandma Rose in the crowd.
Priya kept her team in second place.
Next, Leo dropped the baton when Priya handed it to him.
He picked it up quickly, but another team passed him, so they fell to third place.
Sam ran the last part of the race.
He passed one runner just before the finish line, and their team came in second.

passages.title: The Pancake Breakfast
sentences: By nine o'clock on Saturday, the Lighthouse Café was full of people eating pancakes.
The pancake breakfast was raising money for new library books.
Earlier that morning, Mrs. Lin had shown Leo and Ben how to make the batter.
First, they mixed flour, milk, eggs and a little sugar in a huge bowl.
Then Mrs. Lin heated the flat grill until a drop of water sizzled on it.
Leo poured the batter in circles, and Ben watched for small bubbles on top.
When the bubbles popped, Ben flipped each pancake over.
Leo tried to flip one high in the air, and it landed on the edge of a plate.
At eight o'clock, the doors opened, and the first customers sat down.
By noon, the café had sold three hundred pancakes.
Mrs. Hall, the librarian, said the money would buy forty new books.

passages.title: Setting Up the Concert
sentences: The school concert started at six o'clock on Thursday evening.
At four o'clock, Ms. Gray asked Leo and Sam to help her set up the stage.
First, the boys carried forty chairs from the music room and set them in rows.
Then Leo set up his drum kit at the back of the stage.
He tightened each drum and tapped it to check the sound.
While Leo worked on the drums, Sam placed a music stand in front of every chair.
Next, Ms. Gray tested the microphones.
She said a few words into each one, and Sam told her if he could hear them from the back of the gym.
At five thirty, the band members arrived with their instruments.
Ms. Gray played one note on the piano, and the players tuned their instruments to match it.
When the first song began, Sam sat in the front row with Grandma Rose.

passages.title: Pixel Learns a Trick
sentences: Sam wanted to teach Pixel to roll over.
Before he began, he read a dog training book from the library.
The book said to teach one small step at a time, and to give a treat after each step.
On the first day, Sam asked Pixel to lie down, and Pixel got a treat.
On the second day, Sam held a treat beside Pixel's nose and moved it slowly over his shoulder.
Pixel turned his head to follow it, and then he rolled onto his side.
Sam gave him the treat and said, "Good boy."
On the third day, Sam moved the treat in a full circle, and Pixel rolled all the way over.
By the end of the week, Pixel rolled over when Sam only said the words.
Sam showed the trick to Grandma Rose, and she laughed and clapped.

passages.title: The Whale Spout
sentences: On a calm Saturday in June, Sam and Priya took the ferry to Gull Island.
Halfway across the bay, Captain Ruth Lane spoke over the speakers.
She told everyone to look to the right side of the ferry.
First, Sam saw a tall puff of mist rise from the water.
Captain Lane explained that it was a whale's spout, the air a whale blows out when it comes up to breathe.
Then a long, dark back rose above the waves.
A gull flew over the ferry, and a child near Priya dropped a bag of crackers.
Next, the whale lifted its huge tail into the air and slid under the water.
Priya took three photos, but only the last one showed the tail.
When the ferry reached Gull Island, Sam looked up the whale in a guide book.
It was a humpback whale.

passages.title: The Bean Jar
sentences: Ms. Ortiz gave each student a glass jar, a wet paper towel and three bean seeds.
Ana pressed the paper towel against the inside of her jar.
Then she pushed the beans between the towel and the glass, so she could watch them grow.
She put the jar on a sunny shelf and added a little water every morning.
After three days, each bean split open, and a small white root poked out.
The root always grows first, and it grows down.
Two days later, a pale shoot pushed up toward the light.
On the seventh day, the shoot opened into two green leaves.
Ana drew a picture of her jar every day and wrote the date under it.
At the end of two weeks, she planted the bean in a pot of soil.

passages.title: The Bus Detour
sentences: On Saturday, Sam took the number 4 bus to the library.
Usually, the bus goes along Harbor Road, but that day workers were fixing the road.
A sign at the bus stop said that the bus would take a different way, called a detour.
First, the bus turned up Pine Street, past the bike shop.
Then it drove around the back of the school.
Sam opened a map on his phone and watched a blue dot move along the streets.
Next, the bus crossed the old stone bridge over the creek.
Sam had never been over that bridge on a bus before.
Finally, the bus came down Market Street and stopped in front of the library.
The trip took ten minutes longer than usual, but Sam liked seeing the new streets.
At the library, he borrowed a book of bus and train maps from around the world.

passages.title: How a Frog Grows
sentences: Every spring, the pond behind Harbor Middle School fills with the sound of frogs.
Each frog in that pond started its life in the water, and its body changed shape many times before it could hop onto land.
This change is called metamorphosis, a word that means a change of form.
Ms. Ortiz's class watches it happen every year.
First, a female frog lays a large clump of eggs in shallow water.
Each egg is a tiny black dot inside a ball of clear jelly that protects it.
After one to three weeks, the eggs hatch into tadpoles.
A tadpole has a long tail for swimming and gills for breathing underwater, like a fish.
It spends most of its time eating soft plants and algae.
After several more weeks, the tadpole grows back legs.
A little later, its front legs appear, and its lungs develop so that it can breathe air.
At this stage, the young frog is called a froglet.
Its tail slowly gets shorter, because its body takes in the tail and uses it for energy.
Finally, when the tail is gone, the frog climbs out of the water and lives mostly on land.
For many kinds of frogs, the whole change takes about three months.

passages.title: The Red Moon
sentences: On a clear night in March, the full Moon was going to pass through Earth's shadow.
This is called a lunar eclipse, and it can only happen when the Sun, Earth and the Moon line up in a straight row.
Sam and Priya both wanted to watch it, but from different places.
At nine o'clock, Sam and Grandma Rose drove up to the lookout in Lantern Peaks with a jug of hot chocolate and two folding chairs.
Sam set up the chairs, and Grandma Rose poured the drinks.
At nine thirty, a dark curve began to cover the bottom edge of the Moon.
Sam took a photo every ten minutes, so that later he could study how the shadow traveled across the Moon.
Priya was at the observatory with Dr. Lee that night.
While Sam set up his chairs, Priya helped Dr. Lee point the big telescope at the Moon.
When the shadow started to cover the Moon, Dr. Lee let Priya look through the eyepiece first.
Priya watched the gray craters vanish into the shadow, one after another.
Just before eleven o'clock, the whole Moon turned a dull red color.
Sunlight that passes through Earth's air bends toward the Moon, and the air lets mostly red light through.
Sam sent Priya a text that said, "It's red!"
At that exact moment, Priya sent him the identical words, and they both laughed when they read the messages.

passages.title: The Lost Rover
sentences: At four o'clock, Priya finally heard a faint beeping under a fern near the old mill.
Her rover was there, tipped on its side against a log.
She had been looking for it for more than an hour.
Earlier that afternoon, Priya and Ben had taken the rover to Story Woods to test a new program.
The program let the rover follow a trail by itself.
At two thirty, Priya set it on the path at the campsite and pressed the start button.
For twenty minutes, the rover rolled along the trail while Priya and Ben walked behind it.
Ben stopped once to take a photo of a woodpecker.
Then the rover reached a fork in the trail and turned down the wrong path, toward the creek.
Before Priya could catch up, it rolled behind a large rock and out of sight.
First, the friends searched the bushes near the fork, but they found nothing.
Next, Ben remembered that Priya had added a small speaker to the rover the week before.
Priya opened the rover's control app on her tablet and pressed a button that made the speaker beep.
They followed the sound along the creek all the way to the mill.
Priya turned the rover upright and checked each wheel.
That evening, she changed the program so the rover would stop and wait at every fork.

passages.title: The Second Balloon
sentences: On a still morning in May, Ms. Ortiz's class launched a second weather balloon from the school field.
A weather balloon carries small instruments high into the sky to measure the air.
First, Sam and Priya packed a small box with a thermometer, an air pressure sensor and a tracker that sends out its location.
Next, Maya tied a folded orange parachute to the bottom of the box.
Then Ms. Ortiz filled the large white balloon with helium until it was taller than she was.
Helium is a gas that is lighter than air, so it makes the balloon float upward.
At ten o'clock, the class counted down from ten, and Ben let go of the line.
The balloon rose fast, and in a few minutes it was only a white dot.
As it climbed, the air around it grew thinner, so the balloon slowly grew bigger.
After about two hours, it was more than thirty kilometers high, and it was so big that it burst.
Then the parachute opened, and the box floated down.
While the box was still falling, the class watched its location move across a map on Ms. Ortiz's laptop.
It landed in a field on a farm north of Harbor Town.
That afternoon, the farmer helped them find the box in the tall grass, and the class read the temperatures it had measured.

passages.title: Docking the Ferry
sentences: Captain Ruth Lane has steered the Harbor Town ferry for twenty years, but docking it still takes all of her attention.
On Monday, Ana and Ben watched her from the wheelhouse, the room at the top of the ferry where the captain steers.
Their class was visiting the ferry for a school project about jobs in the harbor.
Ten minutes before the ferry reached Gull Island, Captain Lane slowed the engines.
A big ferry cannot stop quickly, so it must start to slow down long before it reaches the dock.
Next, she turned the ferry so that its front pointed straight at the dock.
While she steered, two crew members walked to the front deck with thick ropes.
As the ferry slid the last few meters, the captain put the engines in reverse, and the ferry stopped beside the dock.
Then the crew threw the ropes to a worker on the dock, who looped them over two metal posts.
Once the ferry was tied tightly, the worker lowered a steel ramp from the dock onto the car deck.
Finally, the cars drove off, one by one, and the walking passengers followed.
Ben said that docking looked harder than any video game, and Captain Lane laughed and agreed.

passages.title: Footprints on the Shore
sentences: On Monday morning, Maya stood on a flat shelf of gray rock below the cliffs and counted twelve giant footprints.
Each print had three wide toes and was longer than her arm.
Dr. Bell said they were made by a large plant-eating dinosaur that walked on three toes.
The prints had been found by accident two days earlier.
On Saturday night, a strong winter storm pushed huge waves against the shore.
The waves washed away a thick layer of sand that had covered the rock for as long as anyone could remember.
On Sunday, a man walking his dog saw the strange holes in the rock and took photos of them.
He sent the photos to the museum, and Dr. Bell called Maya's rock club that evening.
On Monday, the club worked fast, because the next high tide would cover the rock again by noon.
First, Maya and Mr. Varga brushed loose sand out of each print.
Then Dr. Bell measured every print and the distance between them.
The distance between steps shows how fast an animal was moving, and these steps were short and slow.
While the adults measured, Maya drew each print in her notebook, and a seagull watched her from a nearby rock.
Just before the water came back, Dr. Bell pressed soft rubber into the best print to make a copy for the museum.

passages.title: How a Geode Forms
sentences: From the outside, a geode looks like a plain, round, lumpy rock.
When it is cut in half, a hollow space inside is lined with sparkling crystals.
Many geodes take millions of years to form, and the steps happen in a set order.
First, a hollow space forms inside rock.
In some places, gas bubbles are trapped in cooling lava, and the lava hardens around them.
In other places, a hole forms in soft rock when water slowly dissolves part of it.
Next, water seeps into the rock through tiny cracks.
This water carries minerals that are dissolved in it, in the same way that sugar dissolves in tea.
Over time, the water dries up or drains away, and a thin layer of mineral is left on the walls of the space.
This happens again and again, so the layers build up.
Finally, crystals grow from the walls toward the middle, and they keep growing until the space is full or the water stops coming.
Most geode crystals are quartz, which is clear or white, but some are purple amethyst, a kind of quartz.
Maya has a geode in her rock box that Mr. Varga cut open for her with a special saw.
She likes to hold it up to the window, so the crystals catch the light.

passages.title: The Game Jam
sentences: At nine o'clock on Saturday, Mrs. Hall rang a bell, and the library's first game jam began.
A game jam is a contest where teams have a short time to make a whole video game.
Every team had six hours, and the theme was "islands."
Ana, Ben and Maya spent the first half hour planning on a big sheet of paper.
They decided to make a game about a crab that collects shells before the tide comes in.
Then the team split up the work.
While Ben wrote the code that made the crab move, Maya drew the crab, the shells and the beach on a tablet.
At the same time, Ana recorded sounds, such as waves and a short tune on her trumpet for when the crab picked up a shell.
At noon, the team ate sandwiches and tested the first version.
The crab moved, but it walked straight through the rocks.
Ben spent the next hour fixing that problem, while Ana added a timer to the top of the screen.
At two o'clock, they let Leo play the game, and he found that the shells were too easy to collect.
So Maya moved some shells behind rocks, and Ben made the tide come in faster.
At three o'clock, Mrs. Hall rang the bell again, and every team showed its game.
The crab game did not win first prize, but it won the prize for the best sounds.

passages.title: Recording the Song
sentences: When people heard Sam and Priya's song at the spring fair, it sounded as if the two friends had played side by side.
In fact, they had recorded their parts on two separate days, in the small recording studio at the library.
Priya recorded first, on a Tuesday after school.
Before she started, Mrs. Hall showed her how to wear headphones that played a steady click, one click for every beat.
The click helped Priya keep the same speed, or tempo, from the beginning of the song to the end.
She played the cello part three times, and they kept the third try, because it had no mistakes.
On Thursday, it was Sam's turn.
He wore the headphones too, but this time he heard Priya's cello along with the click.
While the recording played in his ears, Sam played his guitar part along with it.
His first try was too fast, so he slowed down and tried again.
A book cart squeaked past the door during the second try, so Sam had to start over.
The third try was perfect.
On Friday, Mrs. Hall helped them mix the two parts, which means making each part loud or soft enough so both could be heard.
Then she saved the song on a small memory stick, and Priya made a label for it.

passages.title: How Maple Syrup Is Made
sentences: Maple syrup starts as a clear, watery liquid inside a tree.
This liquid is called sap, and it carries sugar that the tree made and stored the summer before.
Sugar maple trees give the sweetest sap.
Sap flows best in late winter or early spring, when the nights are below freezing and the days are warmer.
First, a farmer drills a small hole, about as wide as a pencil, into the trunk.
Next, the farmer taps a small spout into the hole.
Sap drips out of the spout into a bucket, or it flows through plastic tubes to a building called a sugarhouse.
A healthy tree can give sap for several weeks without being harmed.
In the sugarhouse, the sap is poured into a wide, flat pan over a hot fire.
As the sap boils, most of the water turns to steam and rises into the air.
The sap slowly becomes thicker, sweeter and darker.
It takes about forty liters of sap to make just one liter of syrup.
Finally, the hot syrup is filtered to remove any grit, and then it is poured into bottles.

passages.title: How a Fossil Forms
sentences: When Dr. Bell's team lifts a dinosaur bone out of the clay cliffs north of Harbor Town, they are holding something that took millions of years to form.
A fossil is the remains or trace of a living thing from long ago, preserved in rock.
Very few animals ever become fossils, because the process needs a long chain of events to happen in exactly the right order.
First, an animal dies near water, such as a river, a lake or the edge of the sea.
Soft parts, like skin and muscle, rot away quickly, so usually only hard parts such as bones and teeth are left.
Next, the bones must be buried quickly by mud or sand, before other animals or the weather can scatter them.
Over thousands of years, more and more layers of mud and sand pile on top.
The weight of those upper layers slowly presses the lower layers into solid rock.
Meanwhile, water seeps through the ground and carries dissolved minerals into the tiny spaces inside the bones.
Slowly, the minerals harden, and the bone turns into a heavy, stony copy of itself.
This step can take millions of years.
Much later, forces deep inside the Earth may push the rock layers upward, and wind, rain or waves slowly wear the surface away.
Only then can the fossil appear again, often at the edge of a cliff or the bottom of a canyon.
Even so, most fossils are found only by people who search very carefully, like Dr. Bell and her team.

passages.title: The Sea Turtle Nest
sentences: On a warm summer night, dozens of baby sea turtles burst out of the sand on a quiet beach and scramble toward the waves.
Each one is small enough to fit in the palm of a hand, and each one must find its own way to the water.
Their journey began about two months earlier, on the very same beach.
First, a female sea turtle swam to shore after dark and crawled slowly up the sand, above the line that the high tide reaches.
With her back flippers, she dug a deep hole shaped like a jar.
Then she laid about one hundred soft, round eggs, each one about the size of a table tennis ball.
She covered the eggs with sand, packed it down firmly and crawled back to the sea.
She never returns to check on her nest, so the eggs develop on their own.
For about two months, the warm sand keeps the eggs at the right temperature.
Surprisingly, the temperature of the sand decides whether most of the babies will be male or female, and warmer nests produce more females.
When the babies, called hatchlings, are ready, each one breaks its shell with a tiny, sharp point on its snout called an egg tooth.
The hatchlings then work together for several days, digging upward until they are just below the surface.
They usually wait until night, when the sand is cooler, before they come out.
Then they head toward the brightest horizon, which on a natural beach is the open sky over the sea.
Once they reach the water, they swim for many hours without stopping, out toward deeper water.
In many places, volunteers cover or switch off beach lights at night, so the hatchlings do not crawl the wrong way.

passages.title: From Rock to Copper Wire
sentences: The copper wires inside a wall, a phone charger or a robot's motor all began as rock deep in the ground.
Rock that contains enough of a useful metal to be worth digging up is called ore.
Most copper ore contains less than one percent copper, so a huge amount of rock must be dug up to make a small amount of metal.
First, miners blast and dig the ore out of a giant open pit, and enormous trucks carry it to a mill.
At the mill, machines crush the rock into pieces the size of gravel, and then they grind the gravel into a fine powder.
Next, the powder is mixed with water and special chemicals in large tanks, and air is bubbled through the mixture.
The tiny bits of copper mineral stick to the bubbles and float to the top as foam, while the waste rock sinks to the bottom.
The foam is dried and then melted in a furnace at more than one thousand degrees Celsius.
Melting separates most of the remaining waste from the metal.
After that, the copper is cleaned even further, until it is almost completely pure.
Finally, the pure copper is shaped into a long, thick rod.
The rod is pulled through a series of smaller and smaller holes, and each pull makes it thinner and longer.
At the end, the copper has become thin wire, which is wound onto large spools, ready to carry electricity.
Mr. Varga keeps a lump of copper ore at the mine museum, so that visitors can compare it with a coil of shiny new wire.

passages.title: The Second Half
sentences: When the final whistle blew, the scoreboard at Pier Field showed Harbor Town 2, Gull Point 2, and the Harbor Town players cheered loudly.
Only an hour earlier, at halftime, the same players had been sitting on the grass, tired and quiet, while Gull Point led by two goals.
The first half had gone badly from the start.
In the fifth minute, Gull Point scored from a long, high kick that sailed over everyone.
Ten minutes later, a strong gust pushed Ana's pass off course, and a Gull Point player scored again.
The wind was blowing hard from the harbor, straight into the faces of the Harbor Town players.
At halftime, Coach Novak knelt on the grass with a clipboard and drew a new plan.
Because the teams would switch ends for the second half, the wind would now be behind Harbor Town.
The coach told the players to keep their passes short and low on the ground, and to let the wind carry their long shots.
While the coach talked, Ben passed around a bag of orange slices, and a dog barked at a seagull near the fence.
Early in the second half, Ben took a long shot, and the wind carried the ball just over the goalkeeper's hands.
After that, the team kept passing short and low, exactly as they had planned.
With three minutes left, Ben slid a short, low pass to Ana, and she scored the tying goal.
On the walk home, Ana said that the tie felt as good as a win.

passages.title: The Beach Robot
sentences: Every spring, volunteers spend a whole Saturday picking up litter on the sandy beach below the lighthouse.
This year, the robotics club wanted to help in a new way.
They spent a month building a robot that could collect bottle caps and other small pieces of plastic.
The robot, which the club named Sweeper, rolled on wide rubber treads that did not sink into the sand.
A camera on its front looked for bright colors.
Then a spinning brush swept anything it found up a small ramp and into a bin.
Before the club brought Sweeper to the beach, Priya tested it on a tray of sand in Ms. Ortiz's science room.
During that test, the brush picked up shells as well as plastic, so Priya changed the program to ignore anything white or gray.
On cleanup day, the club arrived at eight o'clock, and Priya steered Sweeper slowly along the line of dry seaweed at the top of the beach.
While she drove, Ben walked beside the robot with a clipboard and counted every piece it collected.
At the same time, Leo and Maya worked ahead of the robot, picking up larger things by hand, such as cans and an old rope.
Halfway through the morning, Sweeper's battery ran low, so Priya swapped in a spare battery from her backpack.
A seagull followed the robot for a while, and Leo said that the gull must want to join the club.
By noon, Sweeper had collected three hundred and twelve bottle caps and pieces of plastic.
Ben added his count to the volunteers' chart, and the leader of the cleanup asked the club to bring Sweeper back next spring.

passages.title: Mapping the Creek
sentences: Last week, Ms. Ortiz's class made the first detailed map of the creek in Story Woods, from the old mill down to the footbridge.
The finished map now hangs in the library, but making it took three full days of careful work.
On Monday, the class stretched a long measuring tape along the bank, from the mill to the footbridge.
This straight line, called a baseline, gave them something to measure everything else from.
Every five meters along the tape, Sam measured how far it was from the tape to the edge of the water.
While Sam measured, Priya wrote each number in a notebook, and Ben held the end of the tape still.
At the same time, Maya sketched the big rocks, a fallen log and a small pool where tiny fish were swimming.
On Tuesday, it rained so hard that the class stayed indoors, so they studied old maps of Story Woods instead.
Mrs. Hall brought a map from 1950 that showed the creek in a slightly different place, because creeks slowly change their path over many years.
On Wednesday, the class turned their numbers into a drawing.
They chose a scale in which one centimeter on paper stood for one meter of real ground.
First, Sam drew the baseline across a large sheet of paper.
Then the class marked each measurement and joined the marks into a smooth line for the water's edge.
Finally, Maya added her rocks, log and pool, and Priya drew a key that explained every symbol.
Beside their map, the library pinned the map from 1950, so visitors can compare the two.

passages.title: How a Thunderstorm Grows
sentences: On a hot summer afternoon, a small, puffy cloud can grow into a towering thunderstorm in less than an hour.
Scientists describe the life of a thunderstorm in three stages, and the stages always happen in the same order.
The first stage is called the growing stage.
The Sun heats the ground, and the ground warms the air just above it.
Warm, damp air is lighter than the cooler air around it, so it rises.
As it rises, it cools, and the water vapor in it turns into tiny droplets that form a cloud.
Warm air keeps rushing upward, so the cloud grows taller and taller, sometimes more than ten kilometers high.
The second stage, called the mature stage, is when the storm is at its strongest.
The droplets and bits of ice inside the cloud have grown so heavy that they begin to fall as rain or hail.
At the same time, bits of ice and water crash into each other as they rush up and down, and this builds up electric charge.
When the charge becomes strong enough, it is released as lightning.
Lightning heats the air so quickly that the air bursts outward, and this makes the booming sound of thunder.
In the last stage, the falling rain drags cool air down with it.
This cool air blocks the warm, rising air that kept the storm growing, so the storm begins to weaken.
The rain becomes lighter, the lightning stops, and the tall cloud slowly breaks apart.
During any thunderstorm, the safest place to wait is indoors, until the storm has passed.

passages.title: The Guitar Maker
sentences: The guitar maker's workshop smelled of sawdust and varnish, and a row of unfinished guitars hung from hooks along one wall.
Ms. Gray had brought Sam, Priya and Ana there on a Saturday in November, so they could see how an instrument is made.
The guitar maker began by showing them a stack of thin wooden boards.
Before any wood is cut, she explained, it must dry slowly for several years, or the finished guitar may crack.
To make the top of a guitar, she joins two thin boards side by side, and then she cuts the shape of the body from them.
Next, she cuts a round sound hole in the top and glues thin wooden strips called braces underneath.
The braces make the top strong, but they still let it vibrate and make sound.
While the glue dries, she bends the sides of the guitar by pressing thin, damp wood against a hot metal form.
Once the top, back and sides are ready, she glues them together to make a hollow box.
Then she carves the neck from a single block of wood, sets thin metal strips called frets into it, and attaches it to the body.
Several coats of finish protect the wood, and each coat must dry for days before the next one goes on.
Last of all, she adds the strings and tunes them.
Priya asked how long one guitar takes, and the guitar maker said about two months of work, spread over half a year.
Before they left, she let Sam play a few chords on a guitar she had just finished.
Ana said it sounded warmer than any guitar she had ever heard.
On the bus home, Sam wrote the steps in his notebook, so he would remember them in the right order.

passages.title: The Steam Engine
sentences: At exactly eleven o'clock on Sunday, the old steam engine at the Pine Bay Train Museum blew its whistle for the first time in forty years.
Sam covered his ears and grinned, because he had been waiting for that sound since he joined the museum's volunteers two years before.
When Sam joined, the engine was a rusty shell sitting on a short piece of track behind the museum.
The volunteers had already spent a year taking it apart, piece by piece, and labeling every part.
After that, they spent many months cleaning the rust off each part, replacing the worn pipes and repairing the huge boiler.
Sam's job was to paint the wheels, and he gave each of the eight wheels three coats of red paint.
Last spring, the volunteers put the engine back together, and a safety inspector checked every part of the boiler.
On Sunday, the work began long before the whistle.
At five o'clock in the morning, the volunteers lit a coal fire inside the firebox.
The fire heated the water in the boiler, and slowly the water turned to steam.
Steam takes up much more space than water, so the pressure inside the boiler grew higher and higher.
It took nearly six hours for the pressure to become strong enough to move the engine.
While they waited, Sam polished the brass bell, and Grandma Rose handed out cinnamon rolls from her bakery.
After the whistle, the driver opened a valve, and steam rushed into the cylinders and pushed the pistons.
The pistons turned the wheels, and the engine rolled slowly forward, puffing white clouds into the sky.
It traveled only a few hundred meters, but everyone on the platform clapped and cheered.

passages.title: The Space Station Pass
sentences: At 7:42 in the evening, a bright white dot rose above the trees in the west and glided silently across the sky.
It did not blink or flash, which is how Leo knew that it was not an airplane.
It was a space station, a huge spacecraft where astronauts live and work as it circles Earth.
Leo, Maya and Ben had planned this evening for a week.
On Monday, Dr. Hale had told the astronomy club that the station would pass over Harbor Town on Friday, and she had given them the exact time.
She explained that the station can only be seen for a few hours after sunset or before sunrise, when the sky is dark but the station, high above, is still lit by the Sun.
On Thursday, Maya checked the weather forecast and saw that the sky would be clear, and Ben charged his camera.
On Friday at seven o'clock, the three friends hiked up to the lookout with Dr. Hale.
Ben set up his camera on a tripod and pointed it toward the west.
Meanwhile, Maya spread out a blanket, and Leo handed around cups of hot apple juice.
At 7:40, Dr. Hale started a countdown, and two minutes later, the station appeared.
It crossed the whole sky in about five minutes, moving much faster than any star or planet.
The station circles Earth about once every ninety minutes, at a speed of about twenty-eight thousand kilometers per hour.
While the others watched, Ben's camera took one long photo that showed the station as a bright line across the stars.
Then the dot faded and vanished in the east, as the station passed into Earth's shadow.
